lessons.title: Understanding ESD
lessons.body:
Electrostatic discharge (ESD) is a sudden flow of electricity between two objects with different electrical potentials. You feel it when you touch a metal doorknob after walking on a carpetâthat spark is ESD. In electronics, even a tiny discharge you can't feel can destroy sensitive components. A human body can carry up to 25,000 volts of static electricity, but it takes only 10 volts to damage some microchips. In Africa, where dry harmattan winds and dusty conditions are common, static buildup is frequent. For example, in Kano, Nigeria, during harmattan, humidity can drop below 20%, making ESD a daily threat in assembly shops.

ESD damage can be immediate or latent. Immediate failure means the component stops working right away. Latent failure means it works now but fails later, causing returns and lost reputation. Common ESD-sensitive parts include integrated circuits (ICs), microcontrollers, transistors, and LED drivers. You can't see the damage, but it costs money. A single damaged IC in a batch of 100 can ruin a whole production run.

To prevent ESD, you must control static at three levels: the workplace, the person, and the component. Simple steps include using antistatic mats, wrist straps, and storing parts in pink or black conductive bags. In many African workshops, humidity is naturally low, so adding a humidifier or even boiling water in the room can raise humidity above 40% and reduce static. Also, avoid wearing synthetic clothing like nylon or polyester; cotton is safer. When soldering, use a grounded soldering iron tip. Remember: if you can feel a shock, the discharge was at least 3,000 voltsâenough to kill most chips. Treat every component as if it were sensitive, and you'll save time and money.

lessons.title: ESD Protective Equipment
lessons.body:
ESD protective equipment is your first line of defense. The most basic item is a wrist strap. It consists of a band that fits snugly on your wrist, a coiled cord, and a resistor (usually 1 megohm) that safely limits current. Connect the cord to a grounded point. Never use a wrist strap without the resistorâit protects you from electric shock. In many African electronics hubs like Nairobi or Accra, you can buy wrist straps for about $5â$10. Test them daily with a wrist strap tester; if the resistance is above 35 megohms or below 0.75 megohms, replace it.

Another key item is ESD-safe gloves. They are made of conductive fibers and prevent static from your hands reaching components. Use them when handling bare boards. Finger cots (rubber or latex) also work but must be antistatic. For footwear, use ESD shoes or heel straps. If you can't afford them, cotton socks and leather shoes are better than rubber soles. In dry climates, avoid plastic sandalsâthey generate static.

Smocks (lab coats) made of cotton or conductive fabric reduce static from clothing. Never wear wool or synthetic sweaters in an ESD-safe area. For storing and transporting components, use antistatic bags (pink poly bags) or black conductive bags. Pink bags are for non-conductive parts; black bags are for conductive parts. Never use ordinary plastic bagsâthey hold static. Also, use antistatic foam for inserting IC pins. In African markets, you can find these at electronics supply stores or online from sites like Jumia or RS Components. If unavailable, you can make a simple wrist strap using a metal watch band and a wire with a 1M resistor, but always test it. Remember: equipment only works if used correctly. Train everyone to wear straps, and check them every morning.

lessons.title: ESD-Safe Workstations
lessons.body:
An ESD-safe workstation is a designated area where static is controlled. The core elements are an antistatic mat, a common ground point, and a wrist strap. The mat should be made of conductive or dissipative material, typically vinyl or rubber, with a surface resistance of 10^6 to 10^9 ohms. Place it on your workbench. Connect the mat to a ground point using a ground cord with a 1 megohm resistor. The ground point can be a copper pipe driven into the earth or the ground pin of a wall outletâbut never use the live or neutral pins. In many African buildings, proper grounding is missing. If you don't have earth ground, use a grounding rod outside or connect to a metal water pipe. Test the ground with a multimeter: resistance should be less than 1 ohm.

The workstation should also have an ionizer if humidity is below 30%. Ionizers blow ionized air to neutralize static on insulators. They cost around $100â$300, but for small shops, a simple humidifier can help. Keep the area clean and free of dust. Use ESD-safe chairs with conductive casters. Avoid plastic chairs, which generate static. Tools like soldering irons must be grounded; use a three-prong plug and check the tip resistance to ground (should be less than 5 ohms).

Organize the workspace: keep components in antistatic bins or bags. Never place boards on ordinary plastic trays or foam. Use a smock and wrist strap at all times. In a typical African workshop, you can set up a basic ESD-safe station for under $200: mat ($30), wrist strap ($10), ground cord ($5), and a multimeter ($50) for testing. If you can't afford a mat, use a metal tabletop connected to ground, but cover it with a dissipative sheet. Mark the area with yellow tape and a sign: 'ESD Protected AreaâWrist Straps Required.' Train everyone to respect it. A good workstation reduces ESD failures by up to 90%.

lessons.title: Handling ESD-Sensitive Components
lessons.body:
Handling ESD-sensitive components requires discipline. Always assume a component is sensitive unless proven otherwise. Before touching any board or IC, put on your wrist strap and connect it to ground. If you don't have a strap, touch a grounded metal object (like a water pipe) for a few seconds to discharge yourself. But this is not a substitute for a strapâit only works for the moment. When picking up a component, hold it by the edges or the body, never by the pins. Pins are the most vulnerable. For ICs, use a vacuum pickup tool or a chip puller. If you must use your fingers, wear ESD gloves.

When removing components from a board, use a grounded soldering iron and desoldering pump. Avoid using hot air rework stations without proper grounding. When inserting components, place them on an antistatic mat first. Never slide components across a benchâfriction generates static. If you need to set a board down, put it on an antistatic mat or in a pink bag. Never stack boards on top of each other; that can cause ESD and physical damage. For storage, use antistatic tubes for ICs, and antistatic bags for boards. In humid African climates, static is less of a problem, but in dry regions like the Sahel, it's severe. During harmattan, increase precautions: use a humidifier, wear cotton, and test your strap hourly.

Transporting components: use conductive tote boxes or bags. Never carry loose boards in a plastic bucket. If you ship components, wrap them in antistatic foam and place in a sealed bag. Label packages with 'ESD Sensitive' stickers. In a small workshop, you can make a simple ESD-safe carrier from a cardboard box lined with aluminum foilâjust ensure the foil doesn't touch pins. When handing a component to a colleague, touch hands first to equalize potential, then pass it. Better yet, place it on a mat and let them pick it up. Remember: one mistake can destroy a $50 microcontroller. Always follow the rules, and when in doubt, ground yourself.

lessons.title: ESD Audits and Monitoring
lessons.body:
Regular ESD audits and monitoring keep your control program effective. An audit is a scheduled inspection of your ESD measures. Do it weekly or monthly. Start by checking wrist straps: use a wrist strap tester to measure resistance. The pass range is typically 0.75 to 35 megohms. If it fails, replace the strap. Test mats and work surfaces with a surface resistance meter (also called a megohmmeter). Place the two probes 10 inches apart on the mat; resistance should be between 10^6 and 10^9 ohms. If it's too low, it's conductive and could shock you; if too high, it's insulative and won't dissipate static. Clean mats with ESD-safe cleanerânever use ordinary soap, which leaves a residue.

Check ground connections: measure resistance from the mat to the ground point. It should be less than 1 ohm. For ionizers, use a charged plate monitor to verify they neutralize static within 2 seconds. If you don't have a monitor, a simple test is to rub a balloon on your hair, bring it near the ionizer, and see if it loses its attraction. Also, monitor humidity with a hygrometer. Keep relative humidity between 40% and 60%. In dry African regions, use a humidifier and log readings daily. If humidity drops below 30%, increase ionizer use or reduce handling of sensitive parts.

Keep records: create a log sheet for daily wrist strap tests, weekly mat tests, and monthly ground checks. In a small workshop, assign one person as ESD coordinator. They should train others and enforce rules. If you find a problem, fix it immediately. For example, if a mat fails, replace it or use a temporary antistatic mat. Audits also include visual checks: no plastic bags, no synthetic clothing, no food or drinks near workstations. After an audit, review findings with the team. In many African electronics startups, ESD failures drop by 70% after implementing regular audits. It takes only 15 minutes a week but saves hundreds of dollars in damaged components.

lessons.title: ESD Training and Compliance
lessons.body:
Training and compliance are the backbone of any ESD control program. Without proper training, even the best equipment fails. Start by training every new employee on ESD basics: what it is, how it damages components, and how to prevent it. Use simple language and local examples. For instance, explain that walking on a dry cement floor in harmattan can build 10,000 volts. Show a damaged IC under a microscope if possible. Training should be hands-on: practice putting on a wrist strap, testing it, and handling a board correctly. In Africa, where many workers learn on the job, short daily toolbox talks (5 minutes) are effective. Use posters in local languages showing 'Ground Yourself Before Touching Boards.'

Compliance means following rules every day. Create a written ESD policy: all personnel must wear wrist straps in designated areas, no eating or drinking at workstations, and all components must be stored in antistatic bags. Post signs. Enforce with regular audits and make compliance part of performance reviews. For small businesses, you can't afford a full-time ESD manager, so assign a senior technician as ESD officer. They check straps each morning and sign a log. If someone forgets, remind them politelyâdon't punish first-time mistakes. Positive reinforcement works better. Offer a small bonus for teams with zero ESD failures per month.

Keep training records: who was trained, when, and on what. Retrain annually or when procedures change. Use free online resources like YouTube videos from ESD Association or NASA. For certification, consider the IPC-A-610 or J-STD-001 standards, but they are costly. Instead, create your own certificate of completion. In many African countries, electronics assembly is growing; a reputation for quality attracts more customers. ESD compliance shows professionalism. Remember: one trained worker can save thousands of components. Make training continuous, and celebrate successes. When everyone understands why ESD control matters, they'll follow the rules even when no one is watching.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: ESD Control for Electronics Assembly in African Workshops

Electrostatic discharge is the silent killer of electronics assembly businesses. A single unseen spark â often below the threshold of human perception â can destroy a microcontroller, degrade a sensor, or create a latent defect that fails in the customer's hands three months later. For African electronics assemblers working with imported components, warranty claims, and thin margins, ESD control is not a compliance checkbox. It is a direct line item on the profit and loss statement.

This Practical Reference lesson consolidates the operational knowledge from the six core ESD lessons into a working document you can print, laminate, and post at the bench. It assumes you are assembling or repairing boards in a workshop environment â from a two-person startup in Kumasi or Nairobi to a 40-station contract manufacturer in Lagos or Cairo â and that your components arrive from Asia or Europe after long, dry transit.

Why ESD Hits African Assembly Businesses Harder

Three factors make ESD risk higher in many African workshops than in established Asian or European facilities:

  • Climate: Low-humidity conditions in highland and Sahelian regions (Addis Ababa, Windhoek, Kano, Harare in the dry season) routinely drop below 30% relative humidity. At 20% RH, a technician walking across a vinyl floor can generate 35,000 volts. At 60% RH, the same action generates roughly 1,500 volts. Humidity is a free ESD control â but you cannot rely on it year-round.
  • Supply chain: Components shipped in non-ESD packaging, re-bagged at informal markets, or stored in open bins lose their protective environment long before they reach your bench.
  • Cost of failure: A failed board returned under warranty costs you the component, the labour, the shipping, and the customer relationship. In markets where trust is the primary sales channel, a single field failure can end a B2B contract.

How ESD Damage Occurs: The Three Failure Modes

Data Table 1: Static Voltage Generation vs. Human Perception

The table below shows the voltages generated by common workshop activities at different humidity levels, and the voltage at which each level of damage occurs. Note that most ESD damage occurs at voltages the technician never feels.

Table 1: Typical static voltages generated and component damage thresholds
Activity At 20% RH At 60% RH Perceived by human?
Walking across vinyl floor35,000 V1,500 VYes (large spark)
Walking across treated ESD floor1,500 V250 VUsually no
Working at a bench6,000 V100 VNo
Removing DIP from plastic tube2,000 V200 VNo
Picking up a plastic bag20,000 V1,200 VSometimes
Sliding on a chair18,000 V1,500 VSometimes
Damage threshold â MOSFET gate10 â 100 VNever felt
Damage threshold â CMOS IC250 â 2,000 VRarely felt

Source: ESD Association, ESD ADV1.0-2023: For the Development of an Electrostatic Discharge Control Program; and Texas Instruments Application Report SSYA010A, Electrostatic Discharge (ESD).

Data Table 2: ESD Protective Equipment â Selection and Cost Guide

This table maps each control measure to its function, typical cost in a workshop context, and the business risk it mitigates. Prices are indicative for a 10-person workshop and will vary by market and import duty.

Table 2: ESD control equipment, function and business justification
Item Function Indicative cost (10-station) Business risk mitigated
Wrist strap + coiled cordBleeds body charge to groundLowCatastrophic failure at the bench
ESD bench mat + ground cordSafe working surface; drains charge from componentsLowâmediumLatent defects during assembly
Common ground point (bus bar)Single verified earth reference for all stationsLowInconsistent protection; audit failure
Ioniser (bench or overhead)Neutralises static on insulators that cannot be groundedMediumâhighDamage from plastic trays, tape, foam
ESD-safe bags and binsProtects components in storage and transitLowDamage before assembly begins
Hygrometer (humidity monitor)Triggers action when RH drops below 40%LowSeasonal failure spikes
Wrist strap testerDaily verification that straps workLowSilent failure of the primary control
Surface resistance meterVerifies mats and floors are in specMediumAudit non-conformance; warranty claims

Source: ANSI/ESD S20.20-2021; ESD Association ESD TR53-01-22: Compliance Verification of ESD Protective Equipment and Materials.

â  SAFETY WARNING â HIGH VOLTAGE AND PERSONNEL RISK

Never connect a wrist strap directly to a mains earth pin, water pipe, or any unverified ground without a 1 megohm (1 MÎ©) safety resistor in series. A direct ground connection can pass lethal current through the technician if they contact live equipment. All ESD grounding must go through a current-limiting resistor and be verified with a wrist strap tester before each shift.

In workshops running from generator or unstable grid power, verify that the earth reference is genuine and not floating. A floating ground gives a false sense of protection and can itself become a shock hazard. Where no reliable earth exists, use a ground-fault-protected outlet or an isolated ESD ground reference, and document the deviation in your ESD control plan.

Practical Application: Building an ESD Control Plan That Survives an Audit

An ESD control plan is a living document, not a poster. The most common audit failures in African workshops are not missing equipment â they are missing evidence that the equipment works. Auditors and customers ask three questions: Is the ground point verified? Are wrist straps tested daily? Are records kept?

Build your plan around the ANSI/ESD S20.20 framework, which requires:

  1. A written ESD control plan naming a responsible person.
  2. Identification of all ESD-sensitive (ESDS) items in the facility.
  3. Documented training for every person who handles ESDS items.
  4. Verification records for wrist straps, mats, ionisers, and ground points.
  5. Corrective action when verification fails.

For a small workshop, the minimum viable plan is a laminated one-page procedure, a daily wrist strap log, a monthly mat and ground verification log, and a named ESD coordinator. This is enough to satisfy most OEM and Tier-1 customer audits, and it costs almost nothing beyond discipline.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Daily: Test your wrist strap before touching any board. Log the result.
  • â Daily: Check that the bench mat is connected to the common ground point.
  • â Every shift: Confirm humidity is between 40% and 60% RH. If below 40%, activate the ioniser.
  • â Every component: Keep ESDS parts in ESD-safe bags or bins until the moment of assembly.
  • â Every board: Handle by the edges only. Never touch connector pins or component leads.
  • â Every workstation: Remove all non-ESD plastics â cling film, styrofoam, ordinary tape, plastic cups.
  • â Monthly: Verify mat surface resistance and ground point resistance with a meter. Record results.
  • â Quarterly: Retrain all staff. Sign and date the training log. Update the ESD control plan.

Further Reading â Free Official Sources

  • ESD Association (ESDA) â free technical articles, Fundamentals of ESD series, and the ESD ADV1.0 glossary. The primary global authority for ESD standards.
  • JEDEC â free access to JESD625 (Requirements for Handling Electrostatic-Discharge-Sensitive Devices) abstracts and related standards.
  • Texas Instruments SSYA010A â Electrostatic Discharge (ESD) â free application report covering ESD physics, damage models, and protection design.
  • STMicroelectronics AN1181 â ESD Considerations for Microcontrollers â free application note with practical handling guidance.
  • ITU Development Sector â resources on electronics manufacturing capacity building in developing regions, including quality and process control guidance.

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills â Electronics Assembly programme. ESD control is a business discipline: every volt you prevent from reaching a component is a warranty claim you never pay.

quiz.q: What is electrostatic discharge (ESD)?
options: A) A sudden flow of electricity between two objects with different potentials
B) A type of electrical current used in circuits
C) A method of testing electronic components
D) A tool for assembling circuit boards
quiz.explanation: ESD is the sudden flow of electricity when two objects with different electrical potentials come into contact.

quiz.q: How many volts can a human body typically carry as static electricity?
quiz.explanation: A human body can carry up to 25,000 volts of static electricity, though it varies with conditions.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an ESD-sensitive component?
quiz.explanation: Integrated circuits are highly sensitive to ESD and can be damaged by low voltages.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a wrist strap in ESD control?
options: A) To keep your hands warm
B) To safely ground your body and prevent static buildup
C) To hold components in place
quiz.explanation: A wrist strap safely grounds the wearer, preventing static charge from building up on the body.

quiz.q: What is the typical resistance value of the resistor in a wrist strap?
quiz.explanation: A 1 megohm resistor is used to limit current and protect the wearer from electric shock.

quiz.q: Which type of bag is recommended for storing ESD-sensitive components?
quiz.explanation: Pink antistatic bags are designed to dissipate static and protect sensitive components.

quiz.q: What is the ideal relative humidity range for an ESD-safe workstation?
quiz.explanation: Maintaining relative humidity between 40% and 60% helps reduce static buildup.

quiz.q: What should you do before touching an ESD-sensitive component if you don't have a wrist strap?
options: B) Touch a grounded metal object
quiz.explanation: Touching a grounded metal object can discharge your body static, but it's not a substitute for a wrist strap.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT part of an ESD-safe workstation?
quiz.explanation: Plastic chairs generate static and should be avoided; ESD-safe chairs are recommended.

quiz.q: How often should you test your wrist strap?
quiz.explanation: Wrist straps should be tested daily to ensure they are functioning correctly.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an ionizer in an ESD-safe area?
options: B) To neutralize static on insulators
quiz.explanation: Ionizers blow ionized air to neutralize static charges on non-conductive materials.

quiz.q: Which clothing material is safest in an ESD-sensitive area?
quiz.explanation: Cotton is less prone to generating static compared to synthetic materials like wool, nylon, and polyester.

quiz.q: What should you do if you drop an ESD-sensitive component on the floor?
options: A) Pick it up quickly with your bare hands
B) Pick it up with pliers
C) Ground yourself, then pick it up by the edges
quiz.explanation: Ground yourself and handle the component by its edges to avoid ESD damage.

quiz.q: What is the recommended surface resistance range for an antistatic mat?
quiz.explanation: Antistatic mats should have a surface resistance between 10^6 and 10^9 ohms to safely dissipate static.

quiz.q: Why is it important to ground soldering irons?
options: B) To prevent ESD damage to components
D) To keep the tip clean
quiz.explanation: A grounded soldering iron prevents static charge from the tip from damaging components.

quiz.q: What is a latent ESD failure?
options: A) A component that fails immediately
B) A component that works now but fails later
C) A component that never fails
D) A component that fails only in cold weather
quiz.explanation: Latent failures occur when a component is partially damaged and fails later, often after shipping.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a sign of ESD damage?
quiz.explanation: ESD damage can cause visible burns, intermittent operation, or complete failure.

quiz.q: What should you use to clean an antistatic mat?
quiz.explanation: Ordinary cleaners can leave residue that affects conductivity; use an ESD-safe cleaner.

quiz.q: How often should you perform a full ESD audit?
quiz.explanation: Regular audits (weekly or monthly) help ensure ESD controls remain effective.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an ESD coordinator?
options: B) To enforce ESD rules and train others
quiz.explanation: An ESD coordinator is responsible for training, auditing, and ensuring compliance with ESD procedures.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a good practice when handling ESD-sensitive components?
options: A) Hold components by the pins
C) Use a wrist strap connected to ground
D) Work on a plastic table
quiz.explanation: A grounded wrist strap prevents static buildup and protects components.

quiz.q: What is the typical cost of a basic wrist strap?
quiz.explanation: A basic wrist strap typically costs between $5 and $10, making it affordable for small workshops.

quiz.q: Why is it important to avoid plastic bags when storing components?
options: B) They generate and hold static
quiz.explanation: Ordinary plastic bags can generate and hold static charge, which can damage components.

quiz.q: What should you do if your wrist strap fails the daily test?
options: D) Use it only for non-sensitive parts
quiz.explanation: A failed wrist strap does not provide protection and must be replaced.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a benefit of an ESD control program?
quiz.explanation: An effective ESD program reduces failures, improves quality, and saves money.

quiz.q: What is the recommended action if humidity in your workshop drops below 30%?
options: B) Use an ionizer or humidifier
quiz.explanation: Low humidity increases static; use an ionizer or humidifier to raise humidity.

quiz.q: How should you pass an ESD-sensitive component to a colleague?
options: B) Place it on a mat and let them pick it up
C) Hand it directly while touching hands first
quiz.explanation: Either placing it on a mat or touching hands first before handing it reduces ESD risk.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a ground cord on an antistatic mat?
options: A) To connect the mat to a ground point
D) To hold the mat in place
quiz.explanation: The ground cord connects the mat to a ground point, allowing static to dissipate safely.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a common source of static in African workshops?
quiz.explanation: Harmattan winds are dry and dusty, creating low humidity and high static conditions.

quiz.q: What should be included in an ESD training program?
quiz.explanation: Effective training combines hands-on practice with relevant local examples to reinforce learning.
